title: Lauren Berlant
keyWorks: Sex, or the Unbearable (with Lee Edelman, 2014)
On the Inconvenience of Other People (2022)
summary: Lauren Berlant (1957–2021) was an American cultural theorist and one of the central voices of affect theory. Berlant studies how people hold on to the dream of "the good life" — a stable job, love, recognition — even when that dream stops sustaining them, and how people live through a crisis that has become everyday.
onEmotions: For Berlant, feelings are above all attachments: we are attached to people, things and scenarios of life, and emotions tell us what is happening to those attachments. The key concept is "cruel optimism": a situation in which the thing we desire gets in the way of our living well, yet letting go of it is frightening, because our whole world rests on it. Berlant stresses that crisis is more often not an explosion but "crisis ordinariness" — a drawn-out tension that people live in day after day. So emotions here are not private malfunctions but ways of adjusting to a world that often wears people down. Berlant offers no heroic ways out — rather, attention to the small ways of catching your breath, holding on and staying in touch with others.

anxiety.text: In the Dardenne brothers' film Rosetta, the heroine whispers to herself before sleep: "You have a job. You have a normal life." Lauren Berlant hears in this the voice of an era in which a normal life is guaranteed by nothing. Your anxiety seems to be about the same thinning ground — and it has its reasons. Berlant offers the concept of the "impasse" — a drawn-out stretch of time when the old scenarios have stopped working and new ones have not yet appeared, and a person lives in heightened alertness, constantly scanning the world for clues. Your anxiety is not an irrational glitch but the way your body adjusts to instability. Knowing this doesn't cancel the anxiety, but it takes the accusation out of it: you are not "worrying too much" — you are feeling a real precariousness that very many people share.
anxiety.practice: Rest your palms on your knees and feel what is holding you right now: the chair, the floor, the wall behind you. Name to yourself one support that, at least today, isn't shaky.

fear.text: "Cruel optimism" is Lauren Berlant's term for when what we desire gets in the way of our living, yet parting with it is frightening. The fear of losing something important is strongest when your whole world rests on it. Berlant explains why: we are attached not simply to people, work or dreams, but to what they promise — to the sense that life has meaning and a continuation. That is why, for Berlant, it is sometimes frightening to let go even of what harms us: it seems that along with it, our very capacity to hope for anything will collapse. Seeing your fear this way means showing yourself some understanding: your fear is not foolish or "too much" — you are protecting a support, however shaky. Then you can slowly, without sudden moves, look for other supports too, so that fear isn't holding up the whole structure alone.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what do I feel would collapse along with the thing I'm afraid to lose? Is there one more support, even a small one?

sadness.text: Not a catastrophe but weather: Lauren Berlant calls "crisis ordinariness" a hardship that comes not as an explosion but as a stretched-out background pressure that people live in day after day. Sadness can be like that too — quiet, everyday, without any particular drama — and that makes it no less real. In The Female Complaint, Berlant explores how people share such feelings in an "intimate public" — a community where strangers recognize themselves in one another's stories and feel: "I am understood." Your sadness is part of a shared experience, not a personal failure. It can be shared: sometimes it is enough to find a text, a song or a person that speaks of the same thing.
sadness.practice: Put on a song in which someone is sad the way you are, and listen to all of it. That is a small "intimate public": you are not alone.

grief.text: A cup no one will wash anymore, summer plans that won't come true — Lauren Berlant reminds us that we are attached not to one person alone but to a whole world of expectations around them. That is why grief is enormous, and it needs space and time. Loss destroys not only the present but also the future that was bound up with it — and that is exactly what makes grief so disorienting. Berlant calls such stretches "impasses": times when the old order of life no longer works and a new one has not yet taken shape, and a person is simply learning to hold on. Not knowing how to go on living is not a failure but an honest state after your world has cracked. An impasse doesn't call for heroism; small, repeated actions that help you get through the day are enough.
grief.practice: Name one small habit that is helping you get through the day right now. You can simply note that you have it.

loneliness.text: "Other people are inconvenient" — one of Lauren Berlant's last books, On the Inconvenience of Other People, starts from this sober thought. Loneliness hurts, and that pain deserves to be taken seriously, but Berlant invites you to look at it from an unexpected side. Other people are always a little inconvenient — they change us, get in our way, fail to match our expectations, and we are just as inconvenient for them. Closeness, for Berlant, is never smooth. Sometimes loneliness is fed by a fantasy of connection where everything will be easy and frictionless — and against it, real, "inconvenient" people seem not enough. You can gently look at your expectations: you don't have to wait for perfect closeness to feel a little less alone. Berlant also writes about "intimate publics" — about how you can feel a sense of belonging even with strangers who share a similar experience.
loneliness.practice: Call one person today with whom your connection is imperfect but alive — just because, for a couple of minutes. Inconvenience is part of closeness too.

anger.text: You work more, yet have less stability — Lauren Berlant writes a great deal about people who were promised "the good life" but never saw the promise kept. Anger is a legitimate response, especially when the world demands more of you than it gives back. Anger often arises where optimism has been disappointed: you invested in something — work, relationships, the rules of the game — and the deal turned out to be one-sided. Berlant calls neither for suppressing such feelings nor for immediately turning them into a fight; rather, for understanding what exactly you were attached to and what did not come true. Then anger becomes not just an outburst but knowledge: it shows you where your trust was not returned.
anger.practice: Finish this sentence out loud: "I'm angry because there was a hope that…" — and listen to what hope stands behind your anger.

shame.text: In a Laurent Cantet film that Berlant analyzes, a man loses his job and for weeks pretends to go to the office. Shame at "not coping" is very common. In the essay "Slow Death" — which is about the gradual wearing-out of people under hard everyday conditions, not about death in the literal sense — Berlant criticizes the familiar idea that each person is fully the master of their own will and responsible for everything that happens to them. When structural difficulties — a shortage of time, money, energy — are explained by the "weak will" of individuals, a shame is born that is actually addressed to the wrong place. Elsewhere, Berlant speaks of "nonsovereignty": none of us fully governs ourselves, and this is not a defect but a shared human condition. Your shame can be lightened a little: part of what you have piled onto yourself belongs not to you but to circumstances.
shame.practice: Open your palms: in your mind, place in the left what depended on you, and in the right what depended on circumstances. Which palm is heavier?

guilt.text: "Manage yourself" is the unspoken demand that, for Lauren Berlant, the modern world makes of everyone, placing on the individual what is shaped by many causes. Guilt can be an honest response to having hurt someone — and then it helps you make amends. But often we feel a different kind of guilt: for not being productive enough, good enough, for "not keeping up" with the life we are supposedly meant to keep up with. Many of our everyday actions are not heroic deeds but simply ways of getting by, and measuring them against an ideal life is unfair. This helps you tell apart where guilt speaks of a concrete act that can be made right, and where it speaks of an impossible ideal that nobody lives up to.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: is my guilt about a concrete act, or about not living up to an ideal? If it's about an act, what one step is possible now?

envy.text: A stable job, upward mobility, reliable intimacy, the feeling that you are in your right place — for Lauren Berlant, this makes up the fantasy of "the good life," which after decades of instability has become almost unattainable for many. Envy often flares up when someone seems to be living exactly like that. Your envy is not pettiness but an attachment to a promise that the world hands out generously and rarely keeps. In that moment, the other person becomes a screen on which the promise seems to have come true. It helps to ask: what promise exactly do I see in their life? It may turn out that you need not someone else's life but one specific thing — peace, recognition, support — toward which you can look for your own path.
envy.practice: Name to yourself in one word the promise behind your envy: security, recognition, love, freedom? Then think where you already have at least a grain of it.

emptiness.text: Flat affect is Lauren Berlant's name for states in which feelings are not vividly expressed but seem to go beneath the surface. It seems as if your feelings have vanished altogether, and this emptiness can be frightening. Berlant suggests not treating this muted quality as an absence of life: it can be a way to wait things out and save strength in a situation that has pressed down for too long. In an "impasse," when the old scenarios no longer work and there are no new ones, a person often seems to freeze — and this is a form of adaptation, not a breakdown. Your emptiness may be a pause you have taken in order to endure. It doesn't need to be urgently filled with meaning. You can simply acknowledge: this is how it is right now, and this, too, is a way of living through a hard time.
emptiness.practice: Imagine that your emptiness is not an absence but an energy-saving mode. What might it be protecting you from right now?

confusion.text: The world is at once very insistent and enigmatic — that is how Lauren Berlant describes the "impasse," a stretched-out time when the familiar "genres" of life, the ready-made scenarios of how things should go, no longer fit. When the world has stopped making sense, it is natural to be confused. In an impasse people don't find a solution straight away: they feel their way forward, improvise, try things, step back. Berlant sees this not as failure but as the ordinary way people adjust to change. You don't need to understand right away what is happening and where to go. Confusion is a state of searching, and work is already happening within it: you are noticing that the old no longer works, and that is the first condition for something new.
confusion.practice: Walk for five minutes with no goal and no route — just wherever your feet take you. This is an impasse in miniature: feeling your way is still moving.

fatigue.text: Eating, dozing, aimless walks — Lauren Berlant calls such acts a "small vacation from the will": they solve nothing but give a breather. Tiredness and burnout are not a personal failure but often the natural result of a long strain. Berlant uses the phrase "slow death," and it is important to understand it correctly: it is not about death literally, but about the gradual wearing-out of people under conditions where everyday life in itself demands too much energy. This wearing-out, for Berlant, is part of "crisis ordinariness": it doesn't look like a catastrophe, so it is easy to miss. Berlant also writes about "lateral agency" — small actions such as eating, resting or distracting yourself, which don't solve the problem but give you a breather, a chance to stop being a "function" for a while. Your pauses are not weakness but a legitimate way of sustaining yourself.
fatigue.practice: What small action gives you at least a few minutes' breather? Allow yourself one such action today — without guilt.

boredom.text: The ordinary, for Lauren Berlant, is not a grey background but a place where unnoticed work is always going on: we adapt, adjust, keep our balance. Boredom seems trivial, but it can be oppressive and draining. Boredom sometimes arises when life is stuck in an "impasse": the old goals have lost their taste, new ones have not yet appeared, and time seems to have stopped. This doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Boredom can be a sign that a former attachment has loosened and is making room for something else. Listening to it means noticing what you are no longer attached to and what you might be looking for.
boredom.practice: Recall what used to absorb you and now doesn't. What might that say about what is changing in you?

joy.text: Lauren Berlant, the author of Cruel Optimism, also takes the funny seriously — how a shared joke helps us bear the awkwardness and mismatches of life. Joy has a place even when there is a lot that is hard around you. Optimism, for Berlant, is the very force that attaches us to the world and lets us move on; it becomes cruel only when the object of desire gets in the way of our living. And joy often arises exactly where a connection truly sustains us: in a conversation, in a shared joke, in a moment when you are briefly free of pressure. Joy is neither naivety nor denial of the crisis, but a sign of a living, nourishing attachment. You can accept it as evidence: this is something that truly sustains me.
joy.practice: What brought you at least a brief joy today? Note to yourself: this is a connection that sustains me.

love.text: Home, making sense, a future — for Lauren Berlant, when we love a person we also love what the bond with them promises. The tenderness you feel is one of the strongest attachments, and in it we are especially open. Berlant writes about this in Desire/Love and Cruel Optimism. That is why love means so much — and why it can be anxious: a whole world rests on it. Berlant also stresses that love is always bound up with "inconvenience": the other never fully matches our expectations, they change us and knock us out of our habits. This is not a flaw of love but its nature. Accepting your tenderness means accepting this openness too, in which you allow another person to change you a little.
love.practice: What promise does this love hold for you — home, peace, joy, a future? Name it to yourself with warmth.

quote.text: When we talk about an object of desire, we are really talking about a cluster of promises we want someone or something to make to us and make possible for us.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

gratitude.text: Plumbing gets noticed when it breaks — and in later work Lauren Berlant suggests looking the same way at the people, habits and relationships that make life possible: they too are "infrastructure." Berlant writes almost nothing directly about gratitude, but extending this thought, it is where you notice that you are being held. Gratitude is the moment when such invisible support becomes visible: a friend who answers your messages, a neighbour, your usual morning walk. In a world where so much wears people down, this is important knowledge: you are not holding on by your own strength alone. Gratitude helps you see the web you are woven into, and treat it with more care.
gratitude.practice: Name three "infrastructures" of your life — people, habits or places — that hold you up, even if you rarely think about them.

hope.text: "Does it nourish me, or keep me stuck?" Lauren Berlant asks this of our hopes in Cruel Optimism, without devaluing the capacity to hope. Hope helps us live, and Berlant takes it seriously. Optimism, for Berlant, is an attachment to what promises to make life better, and there is nothing wrong with that. But sometimes "cruel optimism" arises: hope is directed at the very thing that holds us back — at relationships that exhaust us, a job that drains us, a self-image we can never reach. Giving up such a hope is frightening, because along with it the ability to hope at all seems to vanish. Berlant doesn't shame anyone for this or demand that they drop everything. Hope doesn't need to be killed; it can gradually be shifted toward what truly sustains you.
hope.practice: Think of your hope and notice what your body does: does it open up or tighten? The body often knows before we do whether a hope nourishes or holds us back.

quote.text: A relation of cruel optimism exists when something you desire is actually an obstacle to your flourishing.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

nostalgia.text: A job for life, a home, a future you could predict — Lauren Berlant shows how this postwar fantasy of "the good life" has worn thin in recent decades. Nostalgia can be warm and bitter at once, and Berlant helps you understand why. Nostalgia often longs not so much for a particular time as for the feeling that life has a clear plot and a reliable footing. This is not naivety but an attachment to a sense of security that was — or seemed — possible. Berlant helps you accept nostalgia without turning it into a program: it shows what you need now — stability, belonging. These needs can be respected and given a place in the present, without demanding that the past come back.
nostalgia.practice: What feeling — not event — do you long for when you remember the past? Where in today is there at least a drop of that feeling?

craving.text: Every attachment, for Lauren Berlant, is optimistic: we reach for a thing for the promise hidden in it. A sharp "I want it right now" can sweep over you, and there is nothing shameful in that. A craving, in this sense, is an attachment too, and its promise is relief, a breather, the sense that things are about to become bearable. In the essay "Slow Death," Berlant speaks of "lateral agency": small acts such as eating that don't solve the problem but offer a short break — something like a small vacation from the will itself in an exhausting world. This idea neither justifies the craving nor shames you for it — it helps you hear what the craving is asking for. If behind "I want" stands "I want things to get easier," you can look for another, gentler kind of break while the wave rises and falls.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, ask yourself: what promise do I hear in this "I want" — calm, warmth, a breather? Say it out loud in one word.

quote.text: All attachment is optimistic, if we describe optimism as the force that moves you out of yourself and into the world in order to bring closer the satisfying something that you cannot generate on your own…
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

addiction.text: The rhythm of the day, a way of coping, sometimes even a circle of people — Lauren Berlant shows how much can rest on one attachment, even one that harms. Stepping out of such a circle is hard, and not because of weak character. Berlant's concept of "cruel optimism" describes exactly this situation: what you are attached to gets in the way of your living, yet giving it up is frightening, because your whole familiar world rests on that attachment. In "Slow Death," Berlant shows that the wearing-out of people is not a private moral story but part of "crisis ordinariness": when life keeps exhausting people, they hold on to whatever gives them some kind of breather. Addiction is not a verdict on you as a person but a way of surviving that has become too costly. Such an attachment can be loosened slowly, without bringing the whole world down at once — and better not alone.
addiction.practice: Say out loud what, besides the habit itself, rests on this circle: a time of day, a feeling, people. If you'd like, you can talk about it with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: Nonsovereignty is one of Lauren Berlant's key words: we never fully possess ourselves, and our actions, feelings and bodies keep slipping out of control. The morning after can be doubly hard: your body aches, and your head is spinning with anxiety, shame and fragments of last night. Usually we hold on to the image of a "normal" person who is always together — and a hangover painfully shatters that picture. In On the Inconvenience of Other People, Berlant writes that we are inevitably inconvenient to one another; sometimes we are inconvenient to ourselves as well. A moral hangover is an encounter with your own nonsovereignty, not proof that you are a terrible person. You can get through this morning without passing a verdict on yourself: first take care of your body, and put off the conversations about last night until things feel easier.
hangover.practice: Instead of reconstructing last night, do one simple thing for your body right now — and count it as care, not as payback.

euphoria.text: A "scene," for Lauren Berlant, is a moment in which the world seems to come together for a while and promises that it could always be like this. You seem to be in such a scene right now: everything seems possible, and this is a real, vivid experience; there's no need to be suspicious of it right away. Such scenes are optimistic in the most direct sense: they draw us out of ourselves toward the world. Berlant only notes that optimism becomes cruel when we demand that a moment last forever and carry our whole life. You can simply live through the euphoria — notice what it opened up, which desires, people and plans suddenly became visible — without turning it into a promise that tomorrow is obliged to keep. Then it stays a gift rather than a debt.
euphoria.practice: Look around and remember this scene like a photograph taken without a phone: the light, the faces, the sounds. Let it stay in memory as a gift, not a promise.

crash.text: The scene where everything promised change has ended, and the world has stayed the same — Lauren Berlant describes such returns to the everyday as among the most abrupt. The comedown after a celebration, a success, a bright evening can feel like falling into a void, and it deserves gentleness. Berlant describes "crisis ordinariness": life consists less of highs and catastrophes than of a drawn-out everyday in which we somehow hold on. Berlant calls such stretches an "impasse" — a state in which the old no longer holds and the new has not yet come, and you have to feel your way. The comedown is neither a punishment for joy nor proof that the joy was a deception. It is a transition, and in a transition you are allowed to move slowly, leaning on the simplest things: sleep, food, a familiar route.
crash.practice: Choose one very simple support for today — a walk to the shop, a shower, a call — and do it without demanding that you feel better.

panic.text: Not a heroic way out of a crisis but a way to live through the next minute — that is what interests Lauren Berlant. In a wave of panic this matters especially: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen — and it is genuinely frightening. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Berlant writes about "nonsovereignty": we never fully govern ourselves — the body, feelings and the world constantly intrude on us. Usually this knowledge is unpleasant, but in a moment of panic it can bring a strange relief: right now you don't need to be fully in control of yourself, and you don't need to defeat the wave. You can stop fighting the panic and let it pass, holding on to the simplest supports: the floor under your feet, a long exhale, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Silently name five objects you can see around you.

dread.text: A conversation, a familiar route, someone's hand, a favourite song — Lauren Berlant is interested in attachments that don't promise the meaning of everything but make life livable. There are moments when the question "what is all this for?" rises up and an abyss seems to open beneath your feet; such dread can't simply be brushed aside. For Berlant, it often comes when a big fantasy wears thin — of "the good life," of everything leading somewhere and adding up to a meaningful story. Berlant is in no hurry to replace it with a new big story. Instead there is attention to what holds people up from day to day. Meaning here is not an answer to the abyss once and for all, but a fabric woven together with others. You can let the big question stay open — and still hold on to the small threads.
dread.practice: Do one small thing right now from among those that hold you up day to day: make tea, send a friend a few words, put on a favourite song.

fomo.text: An intimate public is Lauren Berlant's name for a community of strangers bound together by shared fantasies of what a good life should be. A social media feed seems to be the largest such public, and the feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very tiring. Your fear of missing out is neither foolish nor weak but an attachment to a promise of the good life that you are constantly shown and rarely given. Berlant reminds us that behind other people's scenes there is also tiredness, doubt and ordinary crisis — it just stays out of the frame. You can notice which promise exactly is luring you — and ask whether you yourself need it.
fomo.practice: Lift your eyes from the screen and look out the window for a minute. What is happening in your "scene" right now — with no audience and no editing?

sleepless.text: Lauren Berlant thinks a lot about how everyday life wears people down: work, caring for others, uncertainty. By day there's no time to notice; at three in the morning it all returns — louder, darker, lonelier. In "Slow Death," Berlant shows that this wearing-out is not a personal failure but part of the "crisis ordinariness" that very many people carry. Night-time thoughts are an echo of the day's tension that found no room during the day. You don't have to believe them: at night everything feels final, but that is a property of the night, not of the truth. Berlant values small ways of resting from the need to be composed all the time. A sleepless night can become just such a time — with no task of solving anything, simply lying there, deciding nothing.
sleepless.practice: If a thought won't let go, write it on a slip of paper and tell yourself: "I'll look at it in the morning." Then notice the weight of the blanket on your body.

betrayal.text: A cluster of promises — that is how Lauren Berlant describes any attachment: that you will be seen and cared for, that the future will be shared. That is why betrayal wounds especially deeply: what collapses is not only a relationship but also the world that rested on it. When the other breaks these promises, a great deal disappears at once — and even the past suddenly seems unreliable. Berlant stresses that we don't trust out of naivety: without optimism it is impossible to be attached to anything at all. Your trust was not a mistake but a way of living in the world with others. The pain of betrayal is the price of this openness, but not proof that the openness was in vain. You can grieve the broken promises and be angry without giving up your capacity to trust forever.
betrayal.practice: Say out loud one promise that has collapsed for you, and one that still holds in your life. Speak them both.

jealousy.text: A secure place in the world where you are irreplaceable — in Desire/Love, Lauren Berlant shows that love attaches us to this fantasy too, and not only to a person. Jealousy burns and humiliates at the same time: you want to hold on, and you are ashamed of wanting to. Jealousy flares up when this fantasy senses a threat: what is called into question is not only the relationship but the whole structure your life rests on. Berlant also reminds us of "nonsovereignty": in love we never fully control either the other or ourselves. Jealousy is not an ugliness of character but the anxiety of an attachment that feels its own fragility. You can acknowledge this fragility without trying to defeat it through control, and ask: what am I afraid of losing — the person, or the place they give me in the world?
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence to yourself: "If I lose this, I will also lose…" Don't argue with what comes — just listen.

resentment.text: A peculiar optimism — the hope that justice will someday be restored — is something Lauren Berlant finds even in an old grudge. You carry it for years, and it seems to become part of you. Berlant describes life in an "impasse" — a stretch where the old situation is already over and a new form of life does not yet exist. Resentment often holds us in exactly such a stretch: within it, the bond with the person or event that caused the pain continues, hence its optimism. Berlant doesn't call for quickly letting go or forgiving: attachments don't break off on command. You can respect what your resentment preserves — the truth about the harm done — while asking yourself how much room in your life you are willing to give it. Easing a grudge is slow work, not a moral feat.
resentment.practice: What is my resentment still waiting for — an apology, recognition, justice? Put the question to yourself and just name the answer.

heartbreak.text: A shared daily life, plans, a particular way of being in the world — for Lauren Berlant, love always includes a fantasy of the future too. That is why a breakup can feel as if your whole life has collapsed, and that is no exaggeration. When a relationship ends, you lose not only a person but a whole scenario of "the good life" that you were already living in. That is why a broken heart is so disorienting: the familiar cues for how to live an ordinary day have disappeared. Berlant calls such a time an "impasse" — the old genre of life has ended, and a new one has not yet emerged. An impasse doesn't need to be rushed: you can simply stay in it, try small new rhythms, lean on others. Your pain speaks of how strongly you are able to attach — and that capacity stays with you.
heartbreak.practice: Come up with one tiny new ritual for this week — not as a replacement for the past, just your own.

impostor.text: A normal, competent, "proper" person — Lauren Berlant shows that we constantly check ourselves against this image, though it is largely a fantasy. Hence the exhausting fear of being found out any minute: every success starts to seem like an accident. Berlant calls this "normativity." In reality, people live by improvising, adapting, learning as they go. Impostor syndrome is an attachment to a fantasy of complete sovereignty, as if "real" people were fully in command of themselves and their work. But nobody lives like that: we are all nonsovereign and hold on as we go. Your sense that "I'm not quite in my place" is not an exposure but an ordinary truth about being human, which others simply hide better.
impostor.practice: Think of one person you respect and imagine what they might have doubts about. Notice whether this changes how you see yourself.

self_hatred.text: A successful, composed, loved person who copes with everything — Lauren Berlant shows that many of our demands on ourselves grow out of this fantasy of "the good life." An inner voice that judges you mercilessly causes real pain, but its verdict is by no means necessarily true. When life doesn't match this picture, we more often blame ourselves than the picture. Yet, for Berlant, in an exhausting world many people fail to cope not because of personal flaws but because the conditions themselves wear people down. The critic passes a verdict on the person but doesn't see the circumstances. You can move its voice a little further away and ask: by what measure is it judging, and who came up with that measure? You are more than a mismatch with someone else's picture.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase of your inner critic. Next to it, add: "It doesn't take into account that…" — and name one circumstance of your life.

helplessness.text: Lauren Berlant promises no heroic exits but looks closely at how people hold on where circumstances are stronger. Feeling powerless is one of the heaviest feelings, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Berlant writes in detail about people who live inside "crisis ordinariness," where big decisions are out of reach and circumstances are stronger than any one person. But Berlant notices something else too: even where there is no heroic way out, people find ways to hold on — small gestures of care, habits, conversations, breathers. This is "lateral agency" — the capacity to act not directly against circumstances but sideways, in small things. Helplessness tells the truth about the limits of your strength, but not that you can do nothing at all. Sometimes the only available action is to live this day a little more gently, and that, too, is an action.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small action that is within your power right now — pouring some tea, opening a window, sending someone a single word. And do it.

procrastination.text: In the phrase "I can't get started," Lauren Berlant hears not laziness but a request for a breather. It is an agonizing state, especially when everyone around you seems to be working nonstop. Putting things off, for Berlant, is a form of "lateral," sideways agency: a small step aside from the demand to be productive all the time, a pause from the constant effort of will. Procrastination is often exactly such a breather — inconvenient, but understandable. Besides, a task can carry cruel optimism within it: too much seems to depend on it, and starting is frightening. If you see in putting things off a request for rest, or a fear, rather than a vice, it becomes easier to take the first tiny step.
procrastination.practice: Answer two questions out loud: what does this task promise me if I do it — and what am I afraid of finding out if I start? Then make the smallest first move.

uprooted.text: How people greet each other here, when to stay silent, what not to ask — after a move all this must be relearned: for Lauren Berlant, an almost literal "impasse." When you move away or lose your home, you lose not only an address but a familiar way of living. Berlant describes the "impasse" — a time when the old scenarios have stopped working and new ones have not yet taken shape, and you have to feel your way, carefully reading every small detail. Berlant stresses that living in such a stretch is tiring, and this tiredness is not weakness but the price of constant adjustment. At the same time, new attachments are born in an impasse: small rituals, a favourite café, people with whom you can share your bewilderment. Roots don't grow back at once — they slowly grow out of such small things.
uprooted.practice: Notice one small thing in the new place that has already become a little bit yours — a route, a sound, the face of a shopkeeper.

overload.text: Crises, for Lauren Berlant, no longer come and go — they have become a constant background that we are forced to keep responding to. An endless feed, notifications and news can bring you to a state where your head is buzzing and nothing sinks in. Information overload is an almost pure form of this: every piece of news demands a response, and the next arrives before you have had time to feel the previous one. Your overload is not an inability to "manage your attention properly" but an honest reaction to a world that demands too much. Berlant values small ways of stepping out of constant readiness — if only for a little while, if only in small things. A phone put aside is one such way.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down and look at something still for a minute. Notice that the world didn't collapse during that minute.

unreality.text: A recognizable day, familiar scenarios, connections with other people — extending Lauren Berlant's thought, our very sense of reality rests largely on these threads. Sometimes the world, or you yourself, suddenly seem unreal, as if you were looking at everything through glass; it is a strange and frightening experience, and it deserves to be spoken of gently. When life goes on for a long time in a mode of crisis and exhaustion, these threads can wear thin, and the world loses its density. Berlant also writes about "flat affect" — the muted reactions with which people respond to a life that is too strained. Unreality may be a way of muting too much. Reality comes back gradually, through small touches of the world.
unreality.practice: Take an object with a noticeable texture in your hand and silently describe its weight, temperature and surface.

awe.text: Optimism in the broadest sense, for Lauren Berlant, is the force that draws us out of ourselves toward the world, toward what we cannot create on our own. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare feeling in which this force can be seen almost in its pure form. Usually Berlant is interested in how this force gets stuck in exhausting attachments. But awe shows its pure side: you reach toward something without demanding anything of it or trying to possess it. Awe is a reminder that your capacity for attachment is alive, even if everyday life dulls it. It doesn't need to be turned into a plan or an obligation. It is enough to stay near this vastness and notice how, for a moment, the grip of ordinary worries loosens.
awe.practice: Stay another minute near whatever filled you with awe — without taking pictures or doing anything. Just look.

relief.text: We hold on for so long that we stop noticing how much energy it takes — Lauren Berlant writes a lot about tension that becomes a familiar background. Relief is the moment when what was pressing on you finally lets go, and your body exhales by itself, almost without you. Relief makes that effort visible in hindsight — only now is it clear how hard it was. It is one of those precious breathers out of which a livable life in hard times is made. There's no need to devalue it right away with the thought "what if it all starts again." You can allow yourself simply to stay in it, notice your shoulders easing, and acknowledge: you got through it.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body something has let go. Tell yourself: "The hardest part is behind me."

calm.text: Living in constant expectation of the next blow — that, for Lauren Berlant, is how the everyday life of many of us is arranged. That is why calm, in which nothing is required, is of great value, even if at first it can feel unfamiliar, even suspicious. At the same time, Berlant pays close attention to the moments when a person steps out of composure, even briefly, and allows themselves a small vacation from the will — not trying, not keeping up appearances, simply being. Your calm is neither idleness nor naivety but that very breather without which it is impossible to live for long in a tense world. It doesn't need to be explained or earned. It is enough to notice it and let it last.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute without improving anything. If the thought "I really should…" comes up, note it and return to the quiet.

inspiration.text: Encounters, other voices, books, "scenes" in which a different possibility of living suddenly flashed by — Lauren Berlant is interested in where such bursts come from. Inspiration is the feeling that a current has opened up inside you and you want to create. For Berlant, this is a pure form of optimism: the force that draws you out into the world, toward what you cannot yet do on your own but can already sense. What inspires, for Berlant, is not emptiness but connections with others. Inspiration is not only your personal gift but also a trace of your connections with the world. Taking care of it means not demanding an immediate masterpiece from it and not fearing that it will leave. Even if the current dies down, the possibility it opened has already become part of you.
inspiration.practice: Write down where this spark came from: someone's phrase, a place, a book. Keep this note next to your idea.

schadenfreude.text: Someone slips on a flat floor — and we laugh, though it's awkward. In the essay "Comedy Has Issues" (2017), written together with Sianne Ngai, Lauren Berlant reflects on how the funny is bound up with the awkwardness of living together. A prick of pleasure when something goes wrong for someone else is hard to admit even to yourself, but Berlant helps you look at it without moralizing. In life together we constantly get in each other's way, stumble, look ridiculous. Someone else's fall makes us laugh partly because it releases tension: the awkwardness didn't happen to us. Schadenfreude is a similar release, especially in a world where many feel stuck and other people's success weighs on them. This feeling speaks more of your tiredness than of malice. You can notice it — and gently ask yourself what tension it just released.
schadenfreude.practice: Remember the last moment of schadenfreude and say one word quietly: what tension did it ease for a moment — envy, tiredness, the fear of falling behind?

contempt.text: Lauren Berlant's last book came out in 2022, after the author's death, and is called On the Inconvenience of Other People. Contempt seems cold, but beneath it there is often tiredness, irritation or fear. The book's central idea: other people are inevitably inconvenient — they don't fit our expectations, get in our way, demand that we adjust. And we can even be inconvenient to ourselves. Berlant doesn't see this as a problem to be eliminated: inconvenience is the very fabric of life together. Contempt is an attempt to get rid of inconvenience by placing the other "lower," so that they need not be taken into account. That is understandable: it's easier. But Berlant invites something else — bearing the inconvenience without turning it into a verdict. You can ask yourself: what exactly about this person bothers me so much — and what does that say about me?
contempt.practice: Say to yourself: "This person is inconvenient for me because…" — and finish the sentence. Notice how the feeling changes when "they're worthless" turns into "I find them difficult."

disgust.text: "Unbearable" is the word Lauren Berlant and Lee Edelman put in the title of their joint book, Sex, or the Unbearable. Disgust is a sharp "no" the body says before the mind: to a person, a situation, sometimes yourself. There Berlant explores how closeness to other people calls our sense of wholeness into question. An encounter with what is other — a body, habits, needs — is sometimes "unbearable": it disrupts the picture in which we are composed and make sense to ourselves. But Berlant doesn't conclude that we must flee from the unbearable: we live with it all the time, and it is also what keeps our bonds alive. Disgust is a signal that the boundary of your self has been touched. You don't have to be ashamed of it, and you don't have to obey it blindly. You can ask what exactly came too close — and why just now.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and finish to yourself: "This is too close to…" Don't judge the answer — just see which boundary the feeling is guarding.

revenge.text: The pain will go away, justice will be restored, control will return — that, for Lauren Berlant, is what the fantasy of revenge promises. The wish usually comes after a real wound, and in that sense it is honest. Berlant's concept of "cruel optimism" helps you see how it works. Cruel optimism is an attachment to a promise that actually gets in the way of our living well. That is why the fantasy of payback is so appealing — you can replay it for hours. But from Berlant's perspective, such promises rarely come true: the wound remains, and life revolves more and more around the person who hurt you. This is no reproach to your feeling. It tells you where you were hurt and what needs recognition. You can simply ask what revenge really promises — and look for that in other ways, without causing harm: in words, in boundaries, in the support of people close to you.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly do I hope to feel if I get my revenge — peace, strength, recognition? That is the real need. Where else could it be met?

anger_at_loved.text: Closeness, for Lauren Berlant, is always bound up with the hope for a shared story — that the relationship will become a place of rest and understanding; this is the subject of Berlant's essay "Intimacy." When anger at a partner, parents or children breaks out suddenly and shame follows, it often means that life has come apart from that story. But everyday life with others is also friction, tiredness and endless small demands that don't fit into that story. When reality diverges from the expected plot, irritation builds up. Your anger is not proof that there is no love but a signal: your expectations and your strength have come apart from what is happening. This is no reason to lash out at others. It is a reason to notice where you are overloaded, and to look for a breather before the anger spills over.
anger_at_loved.practice: Remember the last time you snapped and ask yourself: what "plot" did I want from my loved one at that moment — and what was I really missing?

ambivalence.text: Ambivalence, for Lauren Berlant, is not a malfunction but the ordinary structure of any attachment: we are attached to people not for a single quality but for a whole cluster of promises. Loving and not being able to stand the same person is one of the most tangled feelings, and admitting to it is frightening. Some of those promises come true, some hurt. That is why the same face can evoke both tenderness and irritation. Berlant notes that culture offers us simple scenarios — "true love" without doubts — and against them ordinary mixed feelings seem like betrayal. Your mixed feelings are more honest than many beautiful stories. They don't need to be untangled right away. You can let both be, and see what each of them is protecting.
ambivalence.practice: Take a small object in each hand: one for a promise this person keeps, the other for one that hurts. Hold both and let go of neither.

guilty_relief.text: Long caregiving for someone ill, an exhausting relationship, constant vigilance — Lauren Berlant calls such drawn-out hardship "crisis ordinariness." When it ends — in a breakup, a departure, the death of a gravely ill loved one — relief is often frightening: how can you feel lightness if you love them? In such a mode a person lives by adjusting and depleting themselves, and often doesn't even notice it. When the tension finally ends, the body lets go, and relief arrives unbidden. Relief doesn't cancel love: it speaks of how long you held on. Berlant stresses that attachments are always mixed. Love, grief and relief can live side by side, and none of them makes the others any less real.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your hand on your chest and tell yourself: "It was a long time. I'm allowed to breathe out — and to go on loving."

indifference.text: Lauren Berlant's 2015 essay is called "Structures of Unfeeling": it is about "underperformed" emotions, which in contemporary culture show up muted, without the familiar drama. Sometimes, where you are "supposed" to feel something, there is silence inside — and that is more frightening than pain. Berlant believes this is not necessarily emptiness: restraint can be a way of bearing too much, a defence of a psyche worn out by constant upheavals. Your indifference is not proof of heartlessness but, perhaps, an energy-saving mode. A feeling may be present, but in a quiet, unrecognizable form. There's no need to squeeze a "proper" reaction out of yourself. You can simply notice what is happening in your body: sometimes something alive turns up beneath the flat surface.
indifference.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and move your attention through your body: shoulders, belly, throat. Is there even a faint movement anywhere? Just note it, without naming it.

escape.text: A job, a place, a role that have long been wearing you down, yet carry your hopes for "the good life" — this is the classic situation of "cruel optimism" in Lauren Berlant's work. The urge to drop everything is born right here, and it can be sudden and strong. This is about wanting to change your circumstances, not about leaving life. Letting go is frightening: the whole familiar world rests on them. The wish to escape is the moment when the body is already saying "I can't go on like this," while the mind is still holding on. But Berlant warns that the dream of escape can itself become a new promise that changes nothing. It helps to ask not "where should I run?" but "what exactly do I need a breather from?" — and where you can get it right now, even a little at a time.
escape.practice: Go for a short walk and on the way ask yourself: what exactly do I need a breather from? Find one tiny form of it that is available this week.

forbidden_attraction.text: Intimacy builds worlds — Lauren Berlant develops this thought in the essay "Intimacy": attraction to a person is also a pull toward the world they seem to promise, toward another life, another version of yourself. When you are drawn to the "wrong" or an unavailable person, it catches you off guard and unsettles you, but there will be no moral verdicts here. Such feelings can be so strong precisely because of this: what speaks in them is not only a particular person but also what you are missing right now. A "forbidden" attraction is neither a verdict on your life nor an instruction to act, but a reason to listen. What promises are hidden in it — freedom, recognition, aliveness, lightness? That knowledge is valuable in itself, whatever you decide next.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name to yourself three words: what "world" does this attraction promise you? Then ask yourself which of them you especially need right now.

quote.text: Intimacy builds worlds; it creates spaces and usurps places meant for other kinds of relation.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

social_anxiety.text: How to behave, what to say, how to look "normal" — in Cruel Optimism, Lauren Berlant describes people who are constantly improvising all of this. Fear of people and their judgment is very common, even though everyone experiences it as if they were the only one. From the outside it seems that others manage this easily. But for Berlant it is shared work: almost everyone in a group is maintaining a fragile balance and trying not to betray their awkwardness. Berlant also stresses that no one is fully "sovereign" — the complete master of their reactions, face, voice. Your stiffness is not a special defect but the visible part of something everyone has. Perhaps the person next to you is finding it hard too. This thought doesn't take the anxiety away, but it makes it less lonely.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time you are among people, find one person with your eyes and imagine that they, too, are improvising a little right now. Notice whether anything changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Is it a drama, a comedy, a crisis, or just a hard period? In the essay "Genre Flailing" (2018), Lauren Berlant describes the state of not knowing which "genre" we are living in. Uncertainty is exhausting: it's unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. The familiar scenarios — how people behave in such cases, what to expect — stop working, and we flail about, trying first one and then another. Berlant doesn't consider this a failure: "flailing" is a normal way of coping when the familiar world has been disrupted and a new form has not yet taken shape. Your bewilderment is not an inability to live but an honest response to unclarity. You don't have to find the right genre straight away. You can allow yourself to try, to make mistakes, and to hold on to small familiar rhythms until the picture clears.
uncertainty.practice: Come up with a working title for this period of your life and say it out loud. Then do one familiar ritual that helps you hold on while the genre is unclear.

waiting.text: A "situation," for Lauren Berlant, is a state of affairs in which, amid ordinary life, something is unfolding that may turn out to matter. Waiting for an answer, results, news is exactly such a situation: time seems to have stopped, yet you have to go on living, and it drains your strength. It is a state of suspension: we don't yet know how things will turn out, but we are already living in anticipation. Berlant notes that in such periods attention sharpens: we look for signs, reread messages, make guesses. Your restlessness is not impatience but a natural reaction to suspended time. But Berlant is also interested in how people still live in such intervals: how they find small ways to catch their breath and stay in touch. Waiting can be not only waited out but also, a little, made into a place to live.
waiting.practice: Choose one activity for today that has nothing to do with the waiting — a walk, cooking, a call to a friend — and agree with yourself not to check for news while it lasts.

regret.text: Study, work, love, family — in the right order and at the right time: Lauren Berlant calls such ideas the "genres" of life. Regret that keeps coming back for years and gives you no peace often measures the past with exactly this ruler: "I should have done it differently." But Berlant stresses that no one lives their life as a fully sovereign author: decisions are made with too little knowledge, strength and time, under the pressure of circumstances. Your regret is not proof that your whole life was a mistake but a trace of what mattered to you. You can ask yourself: do I regret the act itself — or the mismatch with a script that perhaps was never mine?
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and next to it — what you didn't know then and what you were missing. Read it as a description of circumstances, not as an accusation.

longing.text: The rhythm of the days, familiar words, the feeling of being known — Lauren Berlant writes that attachment rests not only on the person but also on what life becomes with them. Your longing is a feeling with an exact address. When the person is not around, it is not a single thread that breaks but a whole fabric of everyday life. That is why longing can be so physical: you miss not only a face but also the way an ordinary evening sounded with them. Berlant stresses that attachment doesn't end along with presence — it goes on organizing our lives. Your longing is not weakness but the continuation of a bond that hasn't yet found a new form. There's no need to rush it; you can gently notice what exactly from that life is especially dear to you.
longing.practice: Recall one small everyday detail with this person that you miss the most — a sound, a phrase, a habit. Stay with it for a minute.

world_pain.text: What happens to us when we constantly watch other people's suffering from afar? This uncomfortable question is posed by the collection Compassion (2004), edited by Lauren Berlant. Pain for those suffering from war, violence and injustice can wash over you every time you open the news. Berlant notes that compassion can both connect people and leave them in the role of spectators — helpless and exhausted. This is no reproach to the feeling, but a description of its trap. Your pain is a sign of a living connection with the world, not of excessive sensitivity. But you don't have to carry it alone and without a break. Berlant values small, doable actions: doing something close at hand, talking, caring — and sometimes putting the feed aside to save your strength.
world_pain.practice: Choose one doable act of care for this week — for someone nearby or for a cause that matters to you. And give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Reaching toward someone means hoping that the world will respond and that there is a place for you somewhere: every attachment, for Lauren Berlant, is essentially optimistic. That is why it hurts so much when the answer is a closed door. Rejection strikes precisely at this hope, which is why it feels wider than a single refusal — as if the whole world had said "no." But from Berlant's perspective, one person's refusal doesn't cancel the capacity for attachment itself: it stays with you and can find other addresses. Berlant also stresses that we don't control other people's responses, and nobody gets love by the formula "deserve it — get it." Rejection is an event in a relationship, not a verdict on your worth. If it hurts, it means you hoped.
rejection.practice: Call or send a few words to someone with whom the connection already exists and is alive. Let the hope that is hurt right now find at least a small response.

abandonment.text: If a whole structure rests on a single support, the fear of losing it is naturally enormous — Lauren Berlant explains this through attachment, which holds up not only relationships but our sense that life has a shape. The fear of being abandoned touches the very foundation: it seems that without this person your whole familiar world will collapse. The threat of losing the object of attachment feels like a threat to that very shape. In their later work, Berlant speaks of "infrastructure" — of how life rests on many connections, habits, places and people, the way a city rests on roads and pipes. Your fear is not "excessive attachment" but a natural response to vulnerability. What can help is not giving up closeness but gently strengthening other supports: friends, activities, rituals.
abandonment.practice: Draw your "infrastructure": you in the centre, and around you the people, places and habits that hold you up. Which one line could you strengthen a little this week?

unrequited.text: Novels, films, songs about unhappy love — in The Female Complaint (2008), Lauren Berlant explores how people recognize their own pain in them again and again. Love that isn't returned hurts in a particular way: the feeling is real, but there is no response. Berlant calls such a space an "intimate public": a community of strangers who feel that their experiences are alike. This is comforting: you are not alone; a great many people have loved and suffered like this. But Berlant also notes the reverse: such stories can keep us in the hope that love will sooner or later redeem everything, if only there is enough of it. Your pain is legitimate and shared by many. And the question can be put gently: what am I expecting from this love — and are there other places in my life where my tenderness can find a response?
unrequited.practice: Put on a song about unreturned love and listen to all of it. What helped its hero go on living — and what of that fits you?

humiliation.text: No one is the full master of themselves, their life, or how they are seen — Lauren Berlant calls this "nonsovereignty." Humiliation is one of the most searing feelings: as if you had been stripped of your dignity in front of others. Humiliation is experienced as a sudden exposure of this nonsovereignty: you couldn't protect yourself, your image ended up in someone else's hands. But Berlant stresses that nonsovereignty is a shared condition, not a personal disgrace. The fantasy of complete control remains a fantasy, and whoever humiliates is also its captive — trying to assert their power at someone else's expense. Humiliation speaks of the situation and of the other person's act, not of who you are at heart. What helps you regain your footing is not pretending nothing happened, but being able to tell someone who will listen about what happened.
humiliation.practice: Tell someone who will listen about what happened, and at the end add out loud: "This says something about how the other person acted, not about who I am."

body_shame.text: "Willpower" and "proper" behaviour — in the essay "Slow Death," Lauren Berlant shows how talk about bodies and weight turns into a moral story in which the individual is responsible for everything. If you are unhappy with your body, it is not your fault. Berlant shows that such rhetoric shifts onto the individual the responsibility for what is largely shaped by living conditions, work, and access to time and rest. The body becomes a screen onto which social anxiety and shame are projected. Your dissatisfaction is largely an echo of this moralizing, not the truth about you. Your body doesn't have to be a project for correction. You can try treating it not as an object of evaluation but as what carries you through life every day.
body_shame.practice: When a critical thought about your body comes up, ask yourself: "Whose voice is this?" — and place your palm where your body worked especially hard today.

illness.text: A sick person is often expected to "fight" and keep up an unfailingly positive attitude, but Lauren Berlant is interested in something else — how to get through the day at all when strength is low. When your body lets you down, your familiar confidence collapses, and it is natural to feel angry, afraid and tired. Berlant offers the concept of "lateral agency": not a heroic action that changes everything, but small ways of getting through the day — eating, resting, distracting yourself, spending time with someone. Berlant stresses that such actions are neither weakness nor defeat, but a way of sustaining life where big solutions are out of reach. There isn't always the strength to "fight." Simple steps are valuable too: getting through this day, giving yourself a pause, accepting help. There is no single right way to be ill. There is your way — and it is enough.
illness.practice: Note one small thing that brought you at least a little relief or pleasure today. That is your "lateral" support.

pride.text: Sustaining a life in an unstable world is also work, and no small amount of it, though it is rarely recognized: Lauren Berlant returns to this thought again and again. Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and there's no need to hide it. Berlant writes about a world in which many live at an exhausting pace, and the promise of "the good life" keeps slipping away. Against this background, what you have managed — to learn, to build, to see something through, or simply to get through a hard period — is especially valuable. Pride is a way of acknowledging your share of that work. Berlant also reminds us that no one acts entirely alone, so healthy pride sits easily alongside gratitude to those who were there. Give this feeling room: it confirms that you are taking part in your own life.
pride.practice: Write down what you are proud of, and add one line: who or what helped you do it. Allow yourself to feel both.

melancholy.text: The time we live in comes to us first as an atmosphere, a mood, and only later takes shape as a story — that is how Lauren Berlant describes the sense of the present. Bright sadness, quiet and almost warm, is exactly such a mood: in it, memory of what has passed, tenderness for what has been lost, and the sense that life goes on all come together. It needs no fixing, no hurrying, no explaining. Berlant is interested precisely in such unobvious states that don't fit into the familiar genres — neither tragedy nor celebration. Bright sadness is not a breakdown but a fine perception of time. You can simply stay in it: notice which images, sounds and memories come with it.
melancholy.practice: Describe your current mood as weather — in a sentence or two, without judgment. What light is in it, what temperature?

quote.text: The present is perceived, first, affectively.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant
